claims.text: Joule heating of the carbon support induces localized thermal gradients in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
Support-induced localized thermal gradients initiate surface premelting in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
Heat-transfer efficiency at the nanoparticle/carbon interface governs progression from premelting to complete melting.
The nanoparticle/carbon interface modulates local heat accumulation.
The nanoparticle/carbon interface modulates electron-phonon coupling.
Interface-mediated heat accumulation and electron-phonon coupling alter the thermal-gradient distribution across a nanoparticle.
Joule heating produces a nonuniform temperature distribution with enhanced heat accumulation at nanoparticle surfaces contacting the carbon support.
Preferential heating lowers the local energetic barrier for surface-atom diffusion.
Lowering the barrier for surface-atom diffusion causes premelting to begin at the nanoparticle surface.
Surface premelting propagates inward as temperature increases.
FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles on a high-thermal-conductivity carbon support will exhibit surface disorder at lower temperatures than particles on a less conductive or inert support.
With further heating, carbon-supported nanoparticles will progress to complete melting more rapidly than the baseline particles.
On an inert substrate or without a significant conductive interface, melting occurs more uniformly and at higher temperatures without early surface-premelting features.
The proposed behavior depends on the thermal conductivity of the carbon support.
The support-mediated effects may diminish when heating is too rapid.
The support-mediated effects may diminish if oxidation occurs.
